LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 112) respecting the storage of food. He said: The Bill which I desire to introduce to the House, in amendment to the Cold Storage Act, has reference to the greatest question now before the people of this country, the cost of living. The need of something of this kind has been brought forward with great prominence in the last few days in connection with the question of the right to destroy $100,000 worth of eggs which have been in cold storage in the vicinity of Montreal. In the United States there has been so much interest in this matter that one of their most prominent men, Henry Cabot Lodge, has introduced" into the Senate of the United States a Bill dealing with it. Mr. Sulzer has also introduced in the House of Representatives a Bill to prevent the sale or transportation in inter-Mr. BLAIN.
state or foreign commerce of articles of food held in cold storage for more than one year, and Mr. Moore, of Pennsylvania, has introduced a Bill to regulate the storage of food supplies in the District of Columbia. The Bill which I introduce differs somewhat from these Bills. Section 11 of the Bill, amending the Cold Storage Act, provides :
11.	That from and after the passing of this Act it shall he unlawful in Canada to keep in storage in any warehouse or other place of deposit for a longer period 'than one year any meat, fish, poultry, game, butter, eggs, oysters or other food products intended for sale or distribution.
Section 12 provides:
12.	That whenever it shall appear to the satisfaction of the Dominion medical health officer or food inspector that any meat, fish, poultry, game, butter, eggs, oysters or other food products kept in storage for a Period under one year, may not be sold or distributed without prejudice to the public health, the said medical health officer or food inspector shall cause such products to be seized and destroyed.
As hon. gentlemen are well aware, there is a prejudice against the cold storage system, but that is a mistake. There is no doubt that, as Mr. Wilson, the secretary of the Department of Agriculture of the United States, says, that system is one of the greatest blessings to mankind. It started in the cold spring house or the cold cellar of the farm and the refrigerator or ice box of the home. In old days the storage of food products in the time of plenty for use in the time of need was practised.' The object of cold storage is to lay up food in time of production for human consumption when the time of production is over. While that system may be used to the public disadvantage, it will, if properly regulated, tend to the balance ot prices. It enables poor people, or people of moderate means to procure the ordinary necessaries of life at a time when they are not being produced. But the storage system should be guarded. In inquiries made by our neighbours to the south it -has been proved that certain articles kept for six months deteriorated. Butter can be kept much longer than eggs. Eggs kept for three months or more will deteriorate, while poultrv taken out of cold storage at the end of three months can hardly be distinguished from fresh-killed poultry. After three months, however, there is a gradual change for the worse. I consider, from the information which I have obtained, that the keeping of food products afteT the time of the year when they can be reproduced is deleterious. Dr. Wiley, chief of the Bureau of Chemistry of the United States Department of Agriculture, gives a list of different foods which can be kept without deterioration for different periods,

according to the nature of the food. I do not claim that this Bill, which I desire to introduce, will cover the whole case. I merely wish to introduce it, as I think it is the duty of an opposition member to bring to the notice of the government any desirable legislation along this line, and I ask the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Inland Revenue to take up this matter either by introducing legislation of their own or by having this Bill sent to a committee.

I think that the hon. gentleman perhaps is mistaken somewhat in speaking of the time in which food is left in cold storage. The time has not so much to do with the deterioration of the food as the regularity or otherwise of the temperature of the cold storage in which it is kept. Cold storage being carried on under the supervision of private individuals is frequently badly managed and the temperature allowed to vary. Therefore, if we had a law compelling cold storage companies to keep the food under proper temperature that might be better than to enact a time limit. Different products require different temperatures, and when all are kept in the same temperature, some are bound to deteriorate and he spoiled. I do not object to this Bill going to a committee, but I would object to a time limit being fixed altogether irrespective of consideration of temperature, and accommodation. Much also depends on the condition in which the food is when placed in cold storage. To destroy food on a certain day irrespective of its condition just because it had been kept a year would be not only unjust but foolish and useless.

bers from every province of Canada with regard to this Bill. There were no dissenting voices in it whatever.

I rise on a question of privilege to draw attention to an article that appeared in the ' Mail and Empire ' of yesterday. It is headed ' Champion of Reciprocity. Simcoe man testifies before Agricultural Committee. Objections raised to method of spreading the propaganda The article is somewhat lengthy, and I will only read the concluding paragraphs:
By this time the members of 'the committee began to inquire why it was that Mr. Johnston had journeyed from his home to preach reciprocity in Ottawa. It finally transpired that Mr.' Schell, the Liberal member for Oxford and chairman of the committee, had arranged for his appearance before the committee. Several of the opposition members protested vigorously against what they thought was an effort on the part of the government to promote its reciprocity propaganda at the expense of the public. The matter may yet be brought to the attention of the House.
I wish to say that this article is entirely misleading, to say the least. Knowing Mr. Johnston as I did, knowing him to be possessed of expert knowledge in the matter of growing fruit, and knowing that he had a very large practical experience

in connection with a successful co-operative association in the county of Norfolk, an experience in these lines perhaps not equalled by that of any other man in Ontario, I thought he would be able' to give valuable information to the Agricultural Committee. I spoke to the hon. member for Norfolk county (Mr. McCall), who occupies a seat on the opposite side of the House, and asked him if he thought Mr. Johnston would consent to come before the committee, and whether he thought it would be wise to have him come. He concurred heartily in the proposition, and said he would see M>\ Johnston and find out whether he would be willing to appear. This was before the holidays. Mr. Johnston consented to come. This article implies that I brought him here to preach the propaganda of reciprocity, an absolutely incorrect imputation. The discussion of reciprocity in the committee was started by a question asked by an opposition member, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). I do not, however, take the full responsibility of bringing Mr. Johnston here. I told the committee about him and his qualifications to appear before them a week ago last Wednesday, and the hon. member for West Durham" (Mr. Thornton), an opposition member, moved that he be invited to appear before the committee. Mr. Johnston was instructed by me by letter as well as in person not to touch 'upon any question that could be construed as a political question or that would be liable to promote a political discussion. What I said can be confirmed by the hon. member for Norfolk.
As there seems to be a desire to cast a reflection on me as a Liberal member for Oxford, that I had some motive other than the country at heart in bringing Mr. Johnston to appear before the committee,
I wish to say that Mr. Johnston is a Conservative in politics. Thus the article throughout seeks to convey an impression on these several points that is entirely misleading.

The minister will recollect that when we adjourned early this morning it was the understanding that the correspondence between the former member for the constituency and the Public Works Department would be produced.

I understood that if there was any correspondence, that objection would not be pressed to-day. I was asked for it by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) who is not now in his place. If he should desire it, I will see that he gets the correspondence, if there be any.
The understanding was that the item should stand until we got that correspondence.

I did not take the request of the hon. member for Peel as one which would be pressed to-day if the correspondence were not here. It would take some time to get it if there be any. I propose giving it to the hon. member for Peel.
My hon. friend did promise to bring down the correspondence as a condition of getting the item through.
Am I not right in saying that the promise was made to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) ? Carried.

My hon. friend (Mr. Pugs-ley), has no right to interrupt me. I did not suggest that the promise was made to any member in particular of this House The promise was made to you, Mr. Chairman, as a condition of getting that item through, that the correspondence was to be produced. The minister said he hoped that hon. members on this sid-g, because of that promise, would help them to get the item through. And, if now he pretends to say that, with that correspondence or without it, he can get that item through, I say it is a direct breach of faith.

I may be misinformed, but I understood that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), was not further to press the point as to the correspondence. If I have been misinformed on that point, I will ask the committee to wait- a few minutes until the deputy minister is here-.
A moment before, the hon. gentleman cried ' Carried.' I understand that he says now that the item stands until the correspondence is produced.

If the hon. gentleman desires it. But I was informed to-day. whether rightly or -wrongly, as I have no means of knowing, that the request for correspondence would not be urged by the hon. member for Peel.
By the hon. member for Peel, because he could not be present.
Quite so. Do other hoc. gentlemen urge it ?

If there is one reason more than another why the correspondence should be brought down, it is that the minister (Mr. Pugsley), does not want to bring it down. For my part, I might have thought that this was all right, but now that I find that the minister does not wish to bring down these papers, I think we should insist upon having them for it seems evident there is a reason for holding them back. No member of this^House can pledge others. We are glad to follow the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), because he takes the right path; still, when he is not here, there are others to see to it that necessary information is secured.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crosby), is right. If he desires the correspondence, and there is any correspondence-I do not know that there is any -when the deputy minister comes I shall be able to give the information to the committee.

Will the minister have the member from the constitu-*

ency here also ?
I understood that the 'lion, member had a very important engagement this afternoon and was not able to be present.
Cannot you let the item stand until he is here ?

I can do anything to oblige hon. gentlemen opposite,-I do not think there is any limit to my ability in that respect. I observe that my hon. friend .for Macleod (Mr. Herron), is here. We might take up the item for Macleod and get' that through to oblige my hon. friend.
Macleod public building, $10,000

This is to make provision for the purchase of a site and towards the erection of a public building at Macleod, Alberta, for post office and customs purposes. Macleod is a place of a good deal of importance. The postal revenue last year was estimated at $10,584-I have not the exact figures for the year. We have not yet purchased the site, but propose to make the purchase out of this vote. The estimate of the population in 1906 was 1,144, but the town has grown very considerably *since that time. It is a place in which, I think, it is necessary in the public interest that a building should be erected for the post office and customs house.
What is the population now ?
I think it is in the vicinity of between 2,000 or 3,000.
What will the building cost ?
I am not sure as to the amount; we propose to put up a nice building, but the plans have not been prepared
Does the minister expect *to go on with the building this summer ?
Not unlikely.
But the minister should know whether he is going on with it or not.

The most I can say (s *that if the money is voted we will endeavour, in the ordinary course, to purchase the site. That done, we will have the plans prepared, and I trust the building will be [DOT]undertaken within the coming year.
How long does it generally Take to get the building started after the money is voted ?
It depends on whether we are held up by the people wanting too "high a price for the site.

I am glad to see how ardently the minister presses this item for Macleod. He made several attempts to get at it last evening, and is evidently going out of his way now to take up this item. I am pleased that he recognizes the importance of the place and the need for the building. I hope that he will show as great energy in proceeding with the erection of the building as he has shown in the passing of the estimate. I notice the sum to be voted is only $10,000. Would the minister be kind enough to say whether any site has been offered to him or whether the department has taken any steps toward securing a site ? Will he appeal to the board of trade or the town council ?-or what steps will be taken to secure a site that will be agreeable to all the people of Macleod ?

No steps have yet been taken toward the purchase of a site, and no location has been determined upon. Of course, nothing can be done until after the appropriation Bill passes placing the amount at the disposal of the department.
The fact that only $10,000 is to be voted means that the minister is only preparing to buy the site, not to go on with the building.
That depends on the cost of the site.
That would not leave much of a balance.

We might get a .site at $2,000 or $3,000, in which case we could let a contract for the erection of a building, coming to parliament, of course, next fall, with a supplementary estimate for the current year.

I have several letters from people owning property in the town, wishing me to bring to the attention of tire minister their wish to sell certain lots. Of these lots, I know little or nothing. The owners put prices upon them the reasonableness of which I am not able to judge.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron), might say at about what figure these are offered ?
Say two business lots with buildings in the centre of the town, $8,000.
In the ordinary course, after the appropriation Bill passes, we would send an expert of the department to examine the different sites, and then take the necessary steps to purchase the .property.
What are the qualifications of this expert?
Thorough knowledge of the value of real estate, and thorough reliability.
How would he get that thorough knowledge in the department?
He has had experience in examining properties all over the country.

I wish to urge upon the minister the great importance of this .building. The post office in the town of Macleod is certainly not a credit to the government of Canada, it is a disgrace to the government. The building is not a fit and proper place for a post office in a town of the importance of Macleod. Macleod has probably 3,000 inhabitants, it is a railway-centre, a judicial centre, and the centre of business in all that locality. The present post office is not even fit to accommodate a town of 300 people. I hope after the item goes through th'at the minister will lose no time in hastening the erection of that building.
I am glad my hon. friend agrees with me that this building is necessary. In that respect it is not an exception to the general rule.

The minister has asked the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Herron) for some information with regard to the site of this building. I would suggest to the minister that he get his information from the hon. member who represents that constituency, and who possesses the confidence of the people who elected him. Certainly he must know something about the values of property in that town. The minister would secure a much greater confidence from the public, and from members on .both sides of this House, if he would, select the hon. member for Macleod and delegate him to report on the values of these various sites.

I would ask the committee to reconsider the item fora public building for Battleford. I have here the whole file which contains the correspondence. There is a letter from Mr. McCraney, who was then the member for the district, which I will read. It is dated the 19th of January, 1907, and is addressed to the then acting Minister of Public Works :
Dear Sir,-With reference to your letter of the 20th ult. regarding my communication to Mr. Oliver as to the establishment of a government building at Old Battleford, I am herewith inclosing you a letter received by me from Mr. A. Champagne, M.P.P., from whom I asked the particulars which you required.
I sincerely trust that the government may see its way clear to granting my request, and would ask that the sum of at least
$25,000 be placed in the estimates for that purpose.
Yours very truly,

Accompanying that letter was a letter from Mr. Champagne, the present member for the district, dated Battleford, January 2, 1907 :
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of yours inclosing letter from Hon. Sydney Fisher re Dominion publio buildings for Battleford, and asking for further information. In reply, I beg to state that the Dominion government has the following offices here: Dominion Land office, telegraph office, immigration office and temporary hall, post office.
The rent being paid at present is as follows: Dominion Land office, $50 per month; telegraph office, $25 per month; immigration office and hall, $35; post office, allowed by the department, $18, actually paid, by postmaster, $25. The revenue of the Dominion Lands office for the year was $54,610.11, and in 1906, $87,363.71. The volume of business transacted in the telegraph office in 1905 was $5,750, and in 1906, $6,107. The post office receipts for the year ending June 30, 1906, was $3,908.40, and the money order business for the same period was issued, $29,359.03, paid $54,325.03, standing tenth in the province^ of Saskatchewan for gross revenue, and third for money orders paid.
It need hardly be pointed out to you that each of the buildings in which the government offices are now located are inadequate to the service rendered, and that a considerable saving in fuel, light and caretaking could be effected by having all the offices in one building.
Battleford is the oldest established town in western Saskatchewan, and has a population of about 1,100, being the largest town in the province west of the Prince Albert branch railway, and is centrally located in the district, being about 80 miles from the west boundary of the province, and has a force of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, a land titles office, an Indian agency, and is destined with the development of the surrounding a country to be a town of cosiderable importance. .	.
I trust that with the above information, you will have no difficulty in securing a grant for the desired public buildings.
I am, yours truly,

Mr. Champagne informs me, as I think I told the committee last evening, that the population is at present about 2,000. There is also a letter from the hon. Mr. Oliver addressed to the acting Minister of Public Works, which I would read if any hon. gentleman desires it.
It would facilitate the progress of the work of the committee if the minister would kindly send over that file of papers, and let us examine it while he takes up another item.
I have no objection to sending the file over to the hon. gentleman.

As one of the committee of this House who last night disputed

this item and was called names, I may say, iby the Minister of Public Works-
Mr. PUGSLEY, Mr. Chairman, I hope my hon. friend did not think I called him any but good names.

The hon. gentleman applied an adjective to me, and to other members of this committee ' sleepy,' to which I take objection. I want to point out that the information we asked for at 11.20 last night has just been handed to us. We did not object to this item by any means, all we wanted to get was the information which has just been handed to us. I withdraw my objection I offered. At the same time, I wish to say that North Battleford is being neglected perhaps more than it should be.
I do not wish to obstruct the progress of the committee, but I propose to look carefully into this correspondence, and would suggest that the committee take up another item, and let this one stand.

I propose leaving a military item and upon that my hon. friend can speak to this as well.
Calgary immigration building, $10,000.

This is to make provision for a new immigration building at Calgary. The quarters at present occupied are reported by the Minister of the Interior to be altogether inadequate for the requirements of the city. Calgary is growing rapidly and the surrounding country is settling up very fast.
Humboldt public building, $25,000.

That is to make provision towards the erection of a public building at Humboldt. The site has been purchased for $3,000. It is 75 feet on the main street with a depth of 132 feet. This building will serve as a post office, customs house and land office.
What is the revenue of the post office?
The post office revenue is $3,700, the customs duties over $7,000, the money orders issued over $36,000, and the money orders paid over $24,000.
What is the population?

The population of the incorporated town is from 1,200 to 1,300. As the minister has said, this will house the post office, customs and land office services. The post office now occupies the third location since its establishment, the postmaster having been obliged to move as the rented premises became more valuable for private purposes.
What is the rent now paid?
For the post office $280. In addition to that I understand that this has been made a port of customs entry, an outport of Regina.
Has it actually been made a port of entry?
The Minister of Customs authorizes me to say he is positive that Humboldt was made an outport of Regina about three years ago.

Will the Minister of Customs say whether it is intended to make it a port of entry? This is very important in these western towns because the people are put to great inconvenience where the town is not a port of customs entry.

My recollection is that Humboldt is already a "port of entry, an outport of Regina. The outport affords all the facilities to the public for the transaction 'of business that are afforded by the port. The outports collect their own revenues, but they are transmitted through the ports to which they are attached simply to save expense and in order that their returns may be supervised by the officials at the main ports who have possibly had more experience. When the outport becomes sufficiently important it is made a port, and makes its returns direct to the department.
Is there a paid official of the government in charge?
Certainly, with all the responsibilities and duties that pertain to a port.
What is the salary?

That depends on the revenue, we have no uniform standard. As a rule, in the new provinces, where the cost of living is greater, we start them at a somewhat higher figure than in the older provinces. Humboldt was made an outport two or three years ago when the Canadian Northern was opened up.
Who asked for this expenditure?
It was urged by the late member Mr. Adamson, in 1907, when there was an item put in the estimates, and also very strongly urged by the present member.
Is there any correspondence in the matter?
There apparently were letters from Mr. Adamson, dated February *25, and March 1, 1907, stating there was pressing necessity for a public building at Humboldt.
Will the letters be presented to the committee ?
Yes, if any gentleman moves for them. Of course it would require three or four horses and a number of carts to bring over from the department all the letters concerning all these public works.

Judging by the number of horses and carts paid for by the government you might engage one of them in that work, but it would be satisfactory to this side if we could even get the information that a boy with a wheelbarrow could bring over. If the minister does not get through with his estimates faster than he did last night I do not think it will require many horses to bring over the information. A page boy could carry all the information we asked for then, but we could not get it.

It would be impossible for the minister to tell in advance what information might be desired, and if the records concerning all the buildings for which votes were taken were-, brought, it would mean immense labour and possibly after all hon. gentlemen would not look at them.
I want all the correspondence before this item is put through. I want the letters from the boards of trade and other bodies and from the gentlemen who have asked for this building in Humboldt.

I shall be very glad on Monday, before this item finally passes to bring any correspondence there is.
Lethbridge public building, $75,000.

As my hon. friend (Mr. Magrath) who represents the district knows this vote is to erect a building which is very much needed. Lethbridge is growing rapidly, and the post office accommodation for the public is very limited indeed. There has been a very strong demand by the people for a building and that demand has been supported very frequently and very persistently by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat.
Is this building to be used for other than post office purposes?

For customs as well.
Llo.ydminster public building, $30,000.

The site has been purchased. The proposed building is for post office, government telegraph office, and land office. The present accommodation is not what ought to be provided in a town of the importance of Lloydminster. Melfort public building, $20,000.
I am told that Melfort has a population of about 1,500, and it is growing rapidly.
What rent do you pay at present?
Moosej aw, new public building, $50,000.

I am sorry we have to expend money for the erection of a new public building in Moosejaw, but our experts advised us that the existing public building is absolutely unsuitable for the requirements of the city and so we have to provide a new one. Moosejaw is growing very rapidly. It has a population to-day of about 15,000, and the business there is very large. What we propose to do is to start the new building on the additional land which we purchased adjoining the old building, and when we get that part finished sufficiently to accommodate the public in it, we shall tear down the old building, and fill up the space by extending the new building to the street line.
Will this $50,000 cover the cost of the whole thing?

No. Of course a building in the west costs somewhat more than a building in the east. The building at Regina, which is a little larger than Moosejaw has cost in the vicinity of $180,000. We want to give it a building as near like the one at Regina as we reasonably can, to afford needed accommodation and at the same time be a credit to the city. We have to build, of course, looking to the future, and there is every reason to look forward to Moosejaw having a population in the near future of 30,000 or 40,000. As evidence of its growth, I may give the revenues for 1908-9:	post
office, $25,601; customs, $47,220; inland revenue, $13,925; making a total revenue of $86,727. At present, even with the existing post office building, we are paying the following rentals: Crown lands office, $2,280; inland revenue, $360; customs, $240; making a total of $2,880. We hope to be able to accommodate all these departments in the new building, thus saving that rent, as well as affording very 'much better accommodation.
Saskatoon, purchase of land for public building, $35,000.

This is to make provision, looking to the future, for the purchase of land either in the town or in its immediate vicinity, for the erection of public buildings, the idea being to provide accommodation for mounted police and other military forces and other departments. The matter has been pressed upon our attention not only by the' hon. gentleman who represents the constituency, but

by Mr. White, the controller of the Northwest Mounted Police. Saskatoon is growing pretty rapidly, and even if we do not utilize the whole of the land for a number of years, we shall make no mistake in buying a considerable area.

Yes, we have bought the land and are making preparations to go on with the work.
We.yburn public building, $30,000.

This is a very important centre.
Strathcona public building, $10,000.

Hon. gentlemen know that Strathcona is a growing city across the Saskatchewan river from the city of Edmonton. We have purchased the land, 66 feet by 132 feet. The building is to be for customs and post office purposes. The population of Strathcona four years ago was close to 3,000. My information is that to-day it is 5,000 or 6,000. The hon. member for Strathcona is here, and would perhaps favour the committee with a few observations.	[DOT]

I might inform the committee that Strathcona is a very important city. It has over 6,000 population, is the university centre of Alberta, and is also the seat of learning for theological colleges. We are looking for great advancement in the near future, and we do not think we are getting too much for this building.
What is the population?

About 2,500. It is the largest and most important town south of the Canadian Pacific railway, on its main line, in Saskatchewan. It is a large raihvay centre. It is about the second or third largest wheat shipping point in the three prairie provinces. The postal revenue from the sale of stamps is over $8,000. I do not know what the customs revenue is, but in the first six months after the office opened it was over $10,000.
The money orders issued last year amounted to $140,000.

There is a very large business done there. It has a half dozen of our principal banks and a local bank, which does the largest business. This building is required for a land office, post office and a customs house.
Vegreville publio building, $20,000.
Perhaps the hon. member for the district will tell us what he knows about Vegreville.

As everybody who knows anything about the west knows, the town of Vegreville is the largest town between Battleford and Edmonton, and is the centre of the best agricultural country in northern Alberta. It has a population at the present time of about 1,200. Four years ago there were only two or three settlers there. The reason I ask for this public building is not to provide work for the people there, because there is no doubt that in order to start the building we shall have to import the labour. The post office is now in a small store, and the postmaster has not the accommodation he should have. There is a large amount of parcel post business done in that country. I have seen no less than three double teams going out with the mail.
Wetaskiwin public building, $25,000.
The population is about 1,700; postal revenue last year, $7,474; money orders issued, $63,000; money orders paid, $36,000.
When was that item first put in the estimates?
Just before the last election?
What rent are we paying now?
$500. The site has been purchased.
When did this first appear in the estimates?

In the session of 1910.
Chilliwack public building, $25,000.
The land has been purchased and the plans are being prepared. My hon. friend who represents New Westminster will agree that this building is a public necessity.
Have tenders been called for yet?
Not yet, but the plans are being prepared.
I ask that because I have heard that an official communication was sent to Chilliwack last June saying that tenders would be called immediately. Was that warranted by the department?
What date?
Early in June last.
I cannot tell. The order was passed for the purchase of the land on the 3rd of June. If my hon. friend will write me a letter I will give him the information.

It is not sufficiently important to trouble the minister with, but I would like to say that possibly there is no place where there is more urgency for a post office than at Chilliwack. That district is glowing very rapidly. Even the word painting which we are accustomed to have from the minister in presenting his items would fail to do justice to the position of Chilliwack. It has made very rapid growth because of the introduction of railways and is now an incorporated city of sufficient importance to furnish business to five banks. The post office at present presents for the use of the public a room only some 12 feet square. If the minister will realize the conditions there with the population of that size trying to despatch and receive their mails in a room 12 feet square he will see there is need for urgency, and if he could take any steps to hasten the calling for tenders he would be doing a great service to the people. I would like to ask, also, whether the amount now provided for will complete?
No, but it will carry us over the next fiscal year.
What was the $6,000 spent for?

For the site.
Crankbrook public building, $25,000.

This is in the constituency of Kootenay. The site has been purchased and the plans are now being prepared. The'postal revenue is $11,517; customs duties, $33,550; money orders issued, $178,917; money orders paid, $47,164. The population in 1908 was 3,500, and it has grown considerably since. If the hon. member who represents Kootenay were here he would endorse my statement that a public building in Cranbrooke is very much needed.
When was this first voted?
Why the delay?
We did not purchase the site until 1908, on the 18th January. Then we had the one lean year, when our revenue fell off, and we were trying to economize.
I desire to ask for some information on this item.
The site lias been purchased and plans for the building are in course of preparation. We hope to" call for tenders before long.

Is it the intention to go on with the work this summer?

_
Yes.
Has the hon. minister received from Mission City a largely signed petition asking for a building there, and what prospect can he hold out?

I am sure the hon. gentleman would feel that it would be quite improper for me to say anything in advance of the estimates which might be brought down beyond saying that the representations of the people of Mission City will have my careful consideration.

I would like to point out that Mission City needs a public building very badly for at least two departments-the post office and the immigration departments. It is a point on the Canadian Pacific railway which immigrants pass through going to Seattle, and where they are very commonly detained, and where, also, immigrants from Seattle are usually detained. At present they have no other accommodation than the station house of the Canadian Pacific railway. The presence of large bodies of these immigrants there is not only very unpleasant for the general passengers, but it is also rather cruel to the immigrants, and gives them a very poor impression of the cpuntry. I do not expect the minister to act on impressions only, or on merely sentimental grounds, but I think that if he would seek the advice, of the Immigration Department that advice would be in line with the request of the people of Mission City for the erection of a public building at that point for post office and immigration purposes.
What is the population of Mission?
I should say about 1,500. That is the population of the village itself, but that figure does not indicate the importance of the place. It is the trade centre for quite a large district.

I will have it looked into.
Duncan public building, $10,000.

This is to purchase a site and to go towards the construction of a building for post office purposes. We pay now a rental of $250. The postal revenue last year was $3,305; money orders issued $26,393, money orders paid $14,929. I have not a statement of the population, but I believe it is a good town.
Fernie public building, $10,000.

This is to finish the payments on this building. We had a building nearly finished when the. disastrous fire occurred which destroyed so large a part of

Fernie. We had to practically begin over again. This is to complete the work.
What is to be the total cost?

The total expenditure to December 20 last, was $27,964.89.
Grand Forks public building, $30,000.

The site purchased for this building covers a whole block, having frontages on four 'streets. We have called for tenders for the building. The contract has not yet been let because it seemed to the department that the only tender received was pretty high and required careful consideration before awarding the contract. We .are having the matter looked into by the chief architect.
Is the idea to advertise again?
Yes, in the hope that we shall have wider competition.
I suppose the minister has no wish to delay this work. He understands the importance of it?
Yes. But the tender was $18,000 higher than the chief architect's estimate; we did not feel that we could properly award the contract, but that it wat better to call for new tenders.
I presume that due allowance was made for the necessary greater expense of construction in the west?

Yes, the chief architect allowed for that.
Greenwood public building, $30,000.
In what position is this?
We have bought the site and the plans are in course of preparation.
What site was bought and what was the price?
The site was bought from Mr. Nelson and consisted of lots 20, 21 and 22, block 5, having a frontage of 75 feet on Greenwood street, and 115 feet on Government street. The price paid was $3,000.
Is it the intention of the government to go on with this work?
Yes.
Are the plans prepared?

They are in course of preparation, and we hope to be able to go on during the coming summer.
Nanaimo public building, extension, $22,000.

This is under contract. It is a very important work, because Nanaimo is a city of a good deal of importance Mr. PUGSLEY.
and the accommodation there is utterly insufficient.
air. DANIEL. What is the population of Nanaimo?
Eight thousand within the city.
Will this complete the work?
No.

What will be the total cost?
air. PUGSLEY. It is estimated at $29,900. This will leave an additional amount of $2,900 to complete the work.
Nelson public building, addition, $7,000.

Hon. gentlemen are aware how important a city Nelson is. It is a large distributing centre for postal business, and the accommodation there is wholly inadequate. The work is a much needed extension of the present building.
Prince Rupert public building, $50,000.
air. PUGSLEY. The site for this building. which is quite conveniently situated, is to be donated to the government by the Grand Trunk Pacific interests.
air. SCHAFFNER. Is the position a good one? Is it central?
air. PUGSLEY. I think it is the very best we could get. We considered two locations, and, with the very best consideration we could give it, we concluded that this was the best. It is not far from the public wharfs and not far from the railway station. It is close to the business centre-right on the public square.
air. SCHAFFNER. Does the Grand Trunk Pacific own the land adjacent to it?
air. PUGSLEY. They did own it, (but I think they sold all the lots, and reserved this for public purposes.
What is the population now?

I understand it is five or six thousand.
air. SHARPE (Lisgar). The other day I asked the minister whether the government had bought any land from the Grand Trunk Development Company. He answered that his department had not. He said he had inquired to see whether other departments had bought any, and had found that the other departments had not bought any land from the development company.
air. PUGSLEY. I think I said my information was that no other department had bought.
air. SHARPE (Lisgar). What other departments did he ask for that informa-' tion?

I tried to think -what departments would ibe likely to buy, and I inquired from the Minister of Interior, and from the Minister of Railways. I could not think of any other department that would be likely to make purchases.
I asked that-the question should ibe allowed to stand, but I see that it has been taken off the orders of the day.
If the hon. gentleman has any idea that any department has made a purchase, and would intimate what department, and where the land is, it would facilitate matters.
The Agricultural Department, this side of Prince Albert. I would like to have that question answered.

I will see the Minister of Agriculture about it to-morrow.
Revelstoke public building, $30,000.

Revelstoke is a very important station on the Canadian Pacific railway, 'being the point at which that railway branches off going down into the district of southern British Columbia. A demand for a public building here has been pressed upon our attention for a considerable time. We have purchased a lot 75 feet by 100, for which we paid some $5,000. We only purchased it after very careful examination and comparison with other lots, and believe we have got it at a reasonable figure. The population of Revelstoke a few years ago was 3,000, it must be considerably more now. The revenue last year was $8,437 ; customs duty, $103,000 ; imports, $367,350. We are paying a rental of $834 for post office and customs purposes.
How far is the building advanced?
We have not entered into a contract yet, we are having the plans prepared.
Can the minister assure me that the work is likely to 'be carried on this summer?
The chief architect tells me that the plans are pretty well advanced. Very likely the building will go on this summer.

I can agree with the minister as to the importance of this town of Revelstoke, which is not only on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, but one of the chief branches of that whole western system starts there going down through the Arrow lakes. It has a very large traffic, and a good deal of tourist trade, besides a growing population.
Vancouver old post office building, alterations and fittings, furniture, &c., $35,000.
Mr, PUGSLEY. This is for the purpose of renovating the old post office building for the accommodation of the inland revenue and the Dominion assay office. The total probable cost, including fittings, furniture, &c., will run to about $54,000.
We have given them already a fine new post office in Vancouver.

Vancouver is a rapidly growing city, and has now a population of nearly 150,000.
Vancouver examining warehouse, $50,060.

We have bought the land, and this is to enable us to call for tenders for the building. We called for tenders once, and we are going to call for new tenders.
Vernon publio building, $30,000.

My hon. friend who represents the district of Yale-Carilboo (Mr. Burrell) knows that Vernon is quite an important town in the midst of a very excellent fruit growing country. It is proposed to provide for a post office, for customs purposes, and also accommodation for the commanding officer, and an armoury for A and B squadrons. The building is under contract. The total estimated cost will be in the vicinity of $55,000.
Is it actually commenced?
The chief architect tells me it is actually commenced.
Will these quarters be amply sufficient for the military purposes ?

I understand so from the militia authorities. The material is to be brick, with stone dressings, and with a stone faced concrete basement, a two-story building, forty feet in depth, and sixty feet frontage.
(Manitoba-Dominion publio buildings

Renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $15,000.
Mr. 'STAPLES. What public buildings in the city of Winnipeg are being repaired?
This is for the whole province.
I understand the old post office in Winnipeg is being repaired to some extent. To what purpose will it be utilized after it is fixed over?

We have had it repaired and renovated for the purpose of giving accommodation to the Customs Department, and also for a branch of the Finance Depart-1 ment. Work was done last year upon the

immigration (building to the extent of $2,590.

Not quite.
Portage la Prairie public building, $18,000.

This is to construct a public building in Portage la Prairie. The site has been acquired. The proposed building is to provide offices for the Inland Revenue and Indian Affairs Departments, and also to provide armour accommodation for squadron ' C ' of the 18th Mounted Rifles and D and E companies of the 9th regiment. The site consists of two lots on Garry street, with a total frontage of 153 feet, purchased from the Housser-Armstrong Company.
Is it a corner lot?
I cannot say, but I think it is because it runs apparently on two streets, Garry and Campbell.
Have the plans been drawn?
They are now completed and have been submitted to the department concerned, for approval. The tenders will be called for right away.
There is no doubt that the building will be gone on with this summer?

None whatever.
Souris public building, $22,000.
This is to erect a public building in Souris. The work is now in progress.
In what year was this put in the estimates?
In the session of 1907-8.
Just before the election?
That seems like the burning of Rome or the great fire in St. John, or the flood.
It was a very famous burning, it saved the life of the late Minister of the Interior. However, they need a building there.

I regret to be here another session and to find the promise the minister gave me-hardly a direct promise, but almost-that there would appear in the estimates of this session an appropriation for a public building in Carman in the constituency that I have the honour of representing. Each session since I have been here I have appealeu to the Minister of Public Works for an appropriation for Mr. PUGSLEY.
the erection of a building there. I might inform the minister that it is a growing town, it has a population of over 2,000 people, it has three banks, it is a railway centre, three railways running into it, it is a municipal centre, the post office revenue is over $4,000 a year, much greater than in other towns for which provision is made, every denomination is represented there with good churches, the town is equipped with very good conveniences, with electric light a water system, and everything required to make its citizens, who are very progressive, comfortable. It possesses every qualification that the minister has laid down as guiding him in the appropriation of moneys for the construction of buildings in towns throughout the country. I do not believe that either the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Finance can advance a single good reason why it should not have a public building. Petitions have been presented to the government asking for a building. I again appeal to the minister to erect a building there. I can see no reason why there should not have been an appropriation for this town long ago. It is the oldest town south of the Assiniboine river in Manitoba, a pioneer town, and I now hope to get an answer from the minister _ that in his supplementary estimates he will make the desired appropriation towards erecting a building in the town of Carman.
Mr. PUGSLEYL The hon. gentleman puts the case so very nicely, and gives such strong evidence that he approves of my course in making provision for public buildings in different sections of the country where they are needed that it would afford me great- pleasure if, at this moment, I could make the announcement that a public building would be erected at Oar-man immediately. I say that in all sincerity. But my bon. friend knows that when I make up my estimates they have to run the gauntlet of my colleagues, particularly of the Minister of Finance, and tlfht I cannot accomplish all I would like even to please my bon. friend.

I do not know on what argument the minister can refuse a building to Carman. He erects buildings in towns like Humboldt, and other towns of that kind, only a year or two old. Carman is 35 or 40 years of age, and I do not know why the minister cannot give me a more definite answer than that. I would ask whether the Minister of Public Works has asked the Minister of Finance to endorse an appropriation for the town of Carman. I believe that if he has done so, the Finance Minister has told him: Yes, that is a deserving town, a growing town, and it should be supplied with a building.

Further consideration in committee on whole of Bill (No. 32), to incorporate the Security Trusts Corporation.-Mr. Martin (Regina).
I wish to say with reference to this Bill-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe, apart from the question which has already engaged the attention of the committee, attention has been drawn to the fact that there is a company of a similar name in Manitoba, and I have discussed the matter with the hon. member for Regina and he agreed the Bill should stand until inquiry be made as to a possible change of name.

That will be all right.
Progress reported.
House in committee on Bill (No. 73), respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company.-Mr. Turriff.

Some of the branches mentioned in this Bill were provided for in the committee without any notice having been given of them in the ' Gazette.' It seems to me that it is establishing a very bad precedent to let these go into the Bill. I think there was another Bill in which the committee did the same thing. The advertisement in the ' Gazette ' is for a good purpose-to give notice to the public where it is proposed to ask for the right to build a railroad. After such notice is given, to insert in a Bill provision for a number of branches for which no notice
Mr. TURRIFF'. While recognizing the force of the remarks made by the hon. member, I may say that two at least of these branches were asked for by the settlers in the vicinity of where it is proposed to build them, so that if it can be arranged that these can go through, I do not think anybody will suffer, while it will be of great advantage to the people in those districts.

One of these branches appears to be 60 miles long. I am not objecting because I think there is any special danger, but just because it has been our disposition always to observe our rules carefully. After watching the granting of charters, especially of late years, I have come to the conclusion that we would be just as safe and would avoid a good deal of work if we granted charters just as they do in the United States-giving power to any company that wanted to build a railway, upon submitting its plans and having them examined and registered, to go on and build the railway. If we go on granting charters at the present .rate, it will become a mere matter of form before very long. What has the Minister of Railways to say about it ?

There is a good deal of. force in what my hon. friend says. But these notices and rules are for the protection of the public, and I suppose for the railways as well. But when a section of the committee, representing the people' in a certain district, after having been made fully aware of the rule as to advertising urged very strongly, so strongly that they convinced the committee, that we ought to waive that rule, and allow them to put in these branches, I think a fairly strong case is made out. In all these cases where a rule is waived, it is reported by the committee' to the House, and I suppose that was done in this case. If we adhered strictly to the rule, these branches could not go in. Speaking practically, what benefit could be derived by anybody if we did that, and what injury can be done to anybody in this case ? If I thought any one was going to be injured, I would say stand by the rule, but the committee, after consideration, thought it better in th'o c and one or two others not to insist on the rule.

I do not think, from our late experience in granting railway charters, that any harm will come from allowing these Bills to pass because one of the strong reasons for the rule, heretofore, was I that we should not charter parallel lines | or give charters which would interfere with

the rights of chartered lines through the same sections. Of late, however, we take very little concern of this objection but grant charters to almost all who ask them. I do not think any serious injury will arise in this case, but I am only speaking of a disposition to contract a loose habit, and these very oases may be used as precedents by some designing individuals with regard to other Bills. If by any possible means we could avoid these toeing used as precedents, there would be less danger from the innovation.

I would feel like going this far, that where there is any real objection to a rule being waived in committee, we ought to insist on its toeing observed. As to what some call free trade in charters, it is difficult to know what is the better method to adopt. Charters have toeen obtained, particularly in the newer portions of the country, by companies which have no apparent intention of building. They get these charters renewed from time to time tout do not build ; and if we were to stick to the practice which existed formerly of protecting companies that had acquired charters, we might never get railways in some particular sections. I have almost come to the conclusion that where three or four people are after a charter in the same territory, we should give a charter to each and let the man who first builds, get the railway. The same thing comes up in approving route maps. One company will get a charter, and a route map, and will sit down on that, and not build the road. Another comes along and it is told to keep off the right of way because the other company has a ronte map approved. I think we should change the method of approving route maps toy approving them only for a limited period.
What atoout a pass?

When there is only one pass, my idea is to give the other railways a right to run over the one which has the charter, and the route map. That is provided in the Railway Act, and I would feel like putting that in the route map approved.
On section 4,

I wish to call attention to another feature, and that is with reference to the rule we laid down for compelling railway companies to make their capital stock ibear some proportion to their length of road. Where you increase the length of a road by several hundred miles, it would seem to me that the capital stock would have to ibe increased also. I do not know whether the branches proposed in this instance would cost sufficient money to require us to reconsider the question of the capital stock or not.

This is a railway that put its capital stock very high in the 'beginning, up to $50,000,000 to start with.
I think they put it very high in order to cover lines they might construct. The other was that line running from Vancouver north to Yukon, which we raised from $1,000,000 to $10,000,000.

The committee boost the amount of capital stock, helping on watering and over-capitalization. Then, when you come down to this House in the afternoon, you find the House criticising the very thing the committee has been doing in the morning.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
House in committee on Bill (No. 75) respecting the McClary Manufacturing Company.-Mr. Beattie.

This is reported by the Private Bills Committee. I do not know what consideration was given to it. I confess it has a rather suspicious look to me when an industrial concern like this asks power to purchase the stock of other concerns of the same nature. It looks as if it were intended to put several concerns into one combine.

In our Railway Committee, when a company asks power to amalgamate with, or purchase, the stock of any other company, it must name the company, or companies. In a case of this kind it may not be possible to do this, perhaps.
The hon. member (Mr. Beattie) in charge of the Bill is not here, but I may say that, under the Companies' Act, every company chartered has this clause.
Is it not a rather wide clause?
This company is not chartered under the Companies' Act, but has a special charter, which, evidently, had not this clause, or the company would not be seeking to insert it.

I think the Bill had better stand.
Progress reported.
House in committee on Bill (No. 51) respecting the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company.-Mr. Crothers.

I gave notice of amendment of subsection (c) of section 1 of this

Bill. The notice is wrongly worded, but I feel sure that- the committee will accept it notwithstanding this error.
What is the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The notice is given that clause 1 of section (c) be amended by striking out the words ' Spring Coulee ' and inserting the words ' Cardston,' and after the word 'westerly ' the words 'to the town of Pincher Creek.'
Mr. HERRON Instead of reading subsection (1) of clause (e), it should read subsection (c) of clause 1.

That was not accepted by the committee.
Mr. HERRON I will explain "why it was not accepted in committee. When this Bill was before the committee on Tuesday last I moved the same amendments that I am offering here. At the request of the lawyer in charge of the company's interest. I did not press the matter to a decision, but allowed it to stand over until he should hear from his company. For some reason there was a meeting of the Railway Committee on Thursday last, I believe, the first held on a Thursday this session. I was, unfortunately, sick and confined toi my room by the doctor's orders. The committee, I think, did not treat. me fairly in passing this Bill in its original form without my consent. When I heard of it I gave notice of the amendment. This is an old charter, one of eleven or twelve years' standing. It gave very broad powers. The country was a cattle country when these people obtained the chapter, but to-day it is a farming country.
There were only a few settlers in there then, and to-day there is a thickly settled country from one end to the other. In the olden days the people did not expect railways, they knew they were not going to get them, therefore, there w.as little interest taken in the charters. But to-day some company is -going to 'build over this identical ground, in fact this summer the same company will build over the proposed line and they are asking for their old powers under a renewed charter, the powers that they had eleven or twelve years ago. They are -asking now for this charter from Cardston to Pincher Creek, a distance of 55 or 60 miles; they are asking for a spread at the starting point between Spring Coulee and Mountain View' for a distance of about 30 miles, that is at the southwest end of the proposed road, going a distance of 55 or 60 miles north. When they land at the north end they ask for another spread of five townships again, where they -strike the railway at the north, that is 30 miles more. W-e know the company could not come to this parlia-96
ment to-day and ask for a new charter granting them these powers and they are trying to revive an old charter with all the powers which they got twelve or fifteen years ago. That is what I object,to, and I dont think it is right to grant an extension to the company with such conditions. I have had protests from people along the line, and from Cardston in particular, against the granting of the extension altogether. The minister has frankly stated this evening his reasons for granting free trade in charters, and I agree with the minister that when they are not getting any exclusive rights, no -harm would he done by renewing an old charter. But I think when the old company is getting the old charter revived, they should comply with the conditions such as they would have to do when they are asking for a new charter. That is all I am asking. I am asking that at the point of starting they be confined to -a distance of 15 miles instead of 30 miles and 'from Cardston to Mountain View. I presume they will strike the Crowsnest branch near the Pincher Station, and -if they do 'they will h-ave to pas-s close by the town of Pincher Creek. The present Canadian Pacific railway station is the centre of the 'spread where they join the Crowsnest road 'at the north, I therefore -ask that they be 'compelled to go through the town of Pin-'cher Creek. Pincher Creek will not put 'them out of their way. I understand that the hon. minister, when he was in the west last summer, promised to put in a fish ladder in connection with the St. Andrew's locks. I would like to know whether he has fully decided to go on with that work next summer, and if so, why there is not an item in the estimates for it?

I have given a good deal of attention to the matter of a fishway in the dam at St. Andrew's rapids, and personally I am in favour of it being put in. We were requested to put that^ fishway in, not only by residents of Manitoba, but also on behalf of residents of the neighbouring state of Minnesota by the American consul at Winnipeg. In conference with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries 1 learned that upon the American side of the boundary, in the Pembina river, which is a branch of the Red river, there is a dam which was erected by American citizens, and which prevents the fish going up the river and coming around again into the province of Manitoba. We are trying to induce the state of North Dakota to put a fish-way in the Pembina river, and we hope it will be done concurrently with our putting one in the Red river at St. Andrew's rapids, so that fish might ascend both the Pembina and Red rivers.

I am very much pleased to hear what the minister says. I may say that this dam in the Pembina river is at Walhalla, and for 30 years we have not been able to get fish in that river because the Americans who own the dam have absolutely refused to put in a fish ladder. I hope the minister will give his

word that he will not put in a fish ladder at St. Andrew's rapids until the other is put in.
Would all our friends in Manitoba be satisfied with that?
They would not?

If our friends in Manitoba would be satisfied with that, and we could use the dam at St. Andrew's rapids as a leverage to induce our American friends to put in a fish-way on the Pembina river, I would be pleased so to use it. However, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has the matter under his consideration, and has been for some time in communication, through his officials with the authorities of the state of North Dakota.

I had this matter before the department on three or four occasions, and I understood that last session the fish-way in the St. Andrew's dam was provided for. I referred to it again in the early part of this session, and had the assurance of the Minister of Public Works and afterwards the assurance of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the work would be done. I concur in the idea that it would be good policy to use the St. Andrew's dam as a leverage to induce the Americans to put a fish-way in the Pembina river as well. At the same time, I hope it will not be long before we have a fish-way at St. Andrew's dam. There is no doubt that both of these dams should have fishways.

This matter shows the benefit that' is likely to result from the treaty that has recently been agreed to. I am inclined to think, as at present advised, that this is a matter that could be referred to the International Joint Commission, because both of these rivers cross the boundary between the United States and Canada, and that they could take action by way of advice or otherwise which would be of great benefit.
As far as I am personally concerned, I feel like leaving the matter in the hands of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who has given me. his word that it will be attended to.
Has that commission authority over the state of Minnesota?

Well, if they have any authority at all, it is within the scope of the treaty, and a treaty is the paramount law. It over-rides all state law, provincial law or Canadian law. Under the American constitution treaties become the supreme law of the United States.
What power have they to enforce their decisions?
The government of the United States is a very strong one.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mr. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I might say a word with regard to the fishways on the Pembina river and the Red river. The question of the Pembina river has been before the department for some time, and we have, in different circumstances, taken some steps to induce the state authorities to remove that dam on the Pembina river. Unfortunately, we have not so far been very successful. However, the commission which was appointed some time ago to investigate the fisheries in Manitoba were instructed by the department to visit that dam and see what steps could be taken to remove it. We are expecting their report very shortly, and shall be prepared to act on their recommendations. In the meantime. it would be, perhaps, advisable that nothing should be done with regard to the dam on the Red river. I do not think that much time will be lost, or that any one will suffer by the delay, and I hope, with the good relations which seem to exist now between the two countries, that better arrangements will be brought about with regard to the fisheries. This Pembina river is not one of those included in the boundaries waters treaty, but it is one which I intend bringing to the attention of the commissioners when the fisheries treaty is accepted by the American authorities. Both governments have the right to extend the provisions of that treaty to some waters which are not included in it. I am now referring to the fish treaty. I hope that the commissioners will agree with me that this river is one of those which should be included in that treaty, and, perhaps, that will be one of the ways in which the matter would be more easily settled; if, in the meantime, we do not succeed in getting it settled in some other way.

While discussing these two fishways, I might remind the minister of another fishway of which I spoke last year, that on the Whitemouth river, entering the Winnipeg river, and which I think he promised to refer to the commission. The Winnipeg river enters just below the Lac du Bonnet, which abounds in fish, and the Whitemouth river extends a distance of some 75 to 80 miles north and south, and there are numbers of settlers all along its shores, and the fish cannot get up. It will cost very little to put a fishway there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am under the impression that this is one of the questions referred to the commission. The report of that commission has not yet been handed to me, but I expect to have it soon, and shall not fail to bear in mind the remarks of my hon. friend.

I am very much pleased with the stand taken by the government in connection with this matter. The people along the Red river have had fish there a great many years, and we allowed the fish to go right down to the United States. The Americans have had all kinds of fish from Canada, and I think it was a very mean piece of business on the part of the United States people to build this dam on the Pembina river and absolutely refuse to put in a fish ladder. I think this government is perfectly justified in standing pat in connection with the fishway on St. Andrew's locks, because in the early days, when the first settlers went into southern Manitoba, they could get all the fish they wanted, but as soon as the dam was put there the fish ceased coming up. I think we would be justified in using that to bring these people to time. They are in the same box as we on account of there being no fish ladder in St. Andrew's lock, so that fish cannot get through to North Dakota. I think that the government are taking a justifiable course.

While speaking on the subject of the locks east of the dam at St. Andrew's locks, as I may not be here when the harbours and rivers are up, I wish to refer to a matter in that connection. The hon. minister will recollect that last year, in the early part of the session, I drew his attention to the necessity of building approaches to the bridge at that dam. In the early part of this session I asked him whether he had provided a sum in the estimates this year for that purpose. Here is the question I asked:

Mr. Bradbury. I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works whether it is his intention to place a sum in the estimates this year for the completion of the bridge at St. Andrew's dam. I understood the hon. gentleman to state distinctly last year that the work was to be proceeded with immediately; but since then nothing has been done, the approaches have not been built, and the bridge is standing there useless, so far as the public on either side of the river are concerned. It is a very important matter to that part of the province of Manitoba.
To this the minister replied:
I would say to my hon. friend that the work at St. Andrew's rapids was not undertaken for the purpose of affording a bridge across the river, but for the purpose of improving the navigation by the building of a lock and a dam so as to increase the depth of the water between that point and the city of Winnipeg; but it was found, as incidental to the construction of the dam and lock, that provision might be made for the erection of a highway bridge, which would add somewhat to the cost, although the cost would not be nearly so great as it would be if the bridge were undertaken by itself. The work has cost a good deal of money, and up to the present moment the government has not Mr. BRODETJR.
seen its way clear to ask parliament for a vote for the purpose of providing the approaches to what would be the highway bridge. I may say to my hon. friend that there has been no decision arrived at against doing this work. All I can say is that up to the present it has not been decided to ask parliament for an appropriation during the present session.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman how he reconciles that statement with the statement which he made most distinctly on the floor of this House last year, that a sum was going to be placed in the estimates for the building of these approaches.

I do not recall exactly what was said, but I am iucliued to think that any statement which I made was simply an expression of my own opinion; but, of course, in addition to any opinion I might have as to the desirability of going ahead with the work, would be the question of providing the money, a matter which "would rest with my colleagues, and more especially the Minister of Finance.
Now I wish to point out what occurred last session. The minister g^ave me, as I understood, a distinct promise across the floor of this House, that this work should be undertaken. This is a very important-work. About $1,500,000 if I understand correctly, has been spent there already. The bridge stands there to-day about twenty-five or thirty feet up in the air and fully 200 feet away from the highway;- there it stands, a monument to the foolish policy of the Minister of Public Works.
Would my hon. friend tell me how it could have been used as a service bridge for the purposes indicated, except it had been just at the height it is ?

When the plans were prepared, no provision was made for a highway bridge. But to provide the highway bridge I am informed by the minister's own engineers would entail -an extra cost of about $200,000 to strengthen the steel work in connection with that bridge._ But whether it did so or not, the question is not whether the work -could have been-constructed without this bridge or not, but the bridge is there, and the minister promised me that the approaches would be completed, so that the settlers on each side could use it for the purpose for which it was constructed. Now, I wish to refer to what I stated. When the minister was going into Supply last year, I rose to draw attention to this matter, -but as soon as he saw me he understood what I was going to say. I began;
With reference to the bridge over the St. Andrews dam

I got no further, because the minister at once said:

We are going to build that bridge.
I understood what he meant, and he what I meant, and I did not pursue the matter further.
That is just what I want to know.
Yes.

Then I will not discuss it. I am very glad that the minister has seen the necessity of doing that work.
But my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples), did not catch the drift of the conversation .between us, and did not understand the position as well as the minister and I did. He interjected a question :
Does the minister mean that he is going to build the approaches?
The approaches to the bridge.
