Later, when an item was under discussion in my absence from the House-as will be seen on reference to page 6103 ol ' Hansard ' of last year, an item of $55,000 for improvements at St. Andrew's rapids, this matter came up again. The following discussion took place:

The government has been engaged for some time in building a lock and dam at St. Andrew's rapids for the purpose of affording navigation from Lake Winnipeg to the city of Winnipeg. The work is now practically completed, and we expect that in a few days it will be open for navigation.

Does the hon. minister purpose completing the roadway across this superstructure, which I understand is intended to be used as a municipal road? Does he propose making connections with the banks on either side?

What my hon. friend, I suppose, means is, shall we build the approaches so as to enable the people to avail themselves of the bridge, which was built primarily as a service bridge for the lock and dam, as a highway bridge. I may say that we intend to do so.
My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), in requesting the minister to hold that item over, as the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) and I were not present, said:
Perhaps we are not -warranted in asking the minister to withhold the item, but the members for the two constituencies directly interested are not here. My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart) has not yet returned from his Easter holidays, but I understand he will be here on Saturday. My hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) from Selkirk is in the city, but I have been unable to get in touch with
him to have him here while this vote is under consideration. I would like if the minister would permit either of these gentlemen at a later stage to speak on the matter.

X would be very glad to. Both of these hon. gentlemen have already spoken on the question, and 1 am sure that they would regret that there should he any delay in the passing of the item. The hon. member for Selkirk, a short time ago, spoke in very strong terms of the importance of finishing up these approaches and of the very great importance of the work.
Now, if language means anything, surely I am justified in saying that I had a distinct promise from the Minister of Public Works for the completion of this work. He not only tells me across the floor that he intends to complete the work, hut when an item was under discusion two weeks after, for that particular work, he left on the minds of hon. members an impression that if that item went through, it was to provide for the very work that he had promised.
Now, it will be almost an outrage if this matter is allowed to go over this summei without this work being completed. A magnificent bridge has been constructed there, and all that is needed in order to complete it, is the two approaches, one on either side of the river. The absence of these approaches means that about 2,006 people are denied the means of using that bridge, which has been built by the people of this country and which stands there, as I have said, a monument to the foolishness of the policy enunciated by the minister. If he maintains the position that he took in the early part of the session and practically says that the government have not decided what they are going to do in this matter, after giving me a distinct promise across the floor of the House, what reliance are we to place upon the promises of ministers ? I have never doubted, and I hope the minister will not give me rea. son to doubt, that a distinct pledge coming from a minister of the Crown would be openly violated. I do not believe he intends to do so. I do not believe that he recollected that he had made this promise across the floor. I ask him now to redeem that promise, in the interest of the people along that river, and in the interest of the people of this country, who have to furnish this large amount of money already spent. I ask him to go on and construct this work. There must have been some change of policy, because when I was at the locks myself after the session, the engineers led me to believe that tenders had been called for a cantilever bridge to span the lock. So there must have been a change of policy. Whatever it is, I hope the minister will see his way clear to provide the money in the estimates this session, and proceed with that work.

When I had the pleasure of visiting St. Andrews locks a. year ago last summer, I was impressed with the desirability of building the approaches, although I must say that the question as to whether the government should build them or leave the work to the provincial authorities was not entirely free from doubt. It is not so easy as my hon. friend might think to get my colleagues to agree, after building a lock and a dam, and providing that portion of the bridge across a navigable water, to go to the further expenditure of building the approaches to the bridge, which I mav say many provincial and municipal authorities would be extremely glad to construct at their own expense in order to give the needed accommodation to the public. However, after a good deal of hesitation, I decided to recommend to my colleagues to strain a point and to build the approaches for the accommodation of these people living in the municipalities on each side of the river, without calling upon them to bear any portion of the burden. Perhaps I was a little over sanguine as to the time when my colleagues would authorize me to undertake the work. They have not so far given me the requisite monev to enable me to do this work. I may say that my hon. friend himself and some of his associates are not altogether blameless for certain difficulties which have been thrown in my way. I call to mind that at the session before last the hon. member for North Toronto, a leading member of this House, speaking in the presence of the hon. member for Selkirk, charged that that whole work was simply a shameless waste of public money. He used this language:
The Prime Minister is head trustee for the people of Canada. Will he now justify his conduct as head trustee for the people of Canada in sinking

*

. sinking a million and a quarter of money 4n(h'ew's locks? Of that amount, WOO,000 is for a highway bridge, for which no vote was ever taken, and that bridge lies there in its naked steel splendour, thirty-five nr forty feet up in the air from the road on either side. X want to ask the Prime Minister, as head trustee for the people of Canada, to tell me to-night if lie can get anv three businessmen in the city of Winnipeg to Put within his hand any justification, m the traffic that exists at present or in the business which may be expected in the near future, for the expenditure of a million and a quarter of money on that work. Now, Mr. Speaker, when a prominent member of this House, occupying the leading position in the opposition of the hon. Mr. BRADBURY
member for North Toronto, makes the statement that this whole work is simply a waste of public money, and when those hon. gentlemen representing the community especially interested, sit silent and allow that statement to go through this country, it makes the position of the Minister of Public Works much more difficult than it would be if the gentlemen interested Jiad risen in their places and protested against a statement of that kind. The hon. minister has endeavoured, by using the words of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), to let himself down from a very nasty position. There is no question that the member for North Toronto did make the speech the minister refers to, and that speech was referred to bv myself in the House later. I had talked the matter over with the member for North Toronto. What he meant, I think, is this, that there was no justification for the large expenditure that had been made at St. Andrews dam. He did not mean that a dam was not required, lie did not mean that a lock was not required. The position taken by the member for North Toronto and by myself was that this work could have been done for about one-half the money the present government is _ spending upon it. But aside from all this, is the fact that the minister, knowing the conditions, having visited the work himself, knowing that it stands there twenty to thirty feet in the air from either side of the roadway, knowing that there has already been spent in constructing that bridge nearly $200,000, still allows the work to stand out in the middle of the stream quite useless to the people on either side of the river. Now the minister states that he is only one member of the cabinet, and that he cannot obtain this money that he is desirous of obtaining. How does he reconcile this with the fact that when asking a vote of $55,000 in connection with this work he left the inference plainly to be drawn from his language that that'$55,000 included a sum to start that work. He stated distinctly when the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) asked him to allow the vote to stand over until I or the member for Winnipeg returned to the House:

I would, be very glad to. Both of these hon. gentlemen have already spoken on the question, and I am sure that they would regret that there should be any delay in the passing of the item. The member for Selkirk a short time ago- spoke in very strong terms of the importance of finishing up these approaches and of the very great importance of the work.
What other inference could be drawn from that language than that the minister was providing for that work in the estimate before the House? That was my understanding of the question when I was informed of what had taken place. I presumed the work would cost more than $55,000. When a minister asks for public moneys to carry on public works and makes promises, and then his colleagues practically turn him down and refuse to carry out the pledge given by him, that minister is placed in a very awkward position and one which I am sure the Minister of Public Works would not tolerate. The minister, on this occasion, pledged his word. I do not think his colleagues would compel him to violate his word given across the floor of the House, and I hope he will see his way clear to go on with the work.

I regret very much, indeed, that my hon. friend should have sought to misrepresent the representations which I made to this House in 1910, when the item of $55,000 was being obtained. He says I gave the committee to understand that the vote I was then asking would enable me to go on with the building of the approaches of the bridge. I would ask him to look at page 6103 of the ' Hansard ' of 1910, where he will find:

There is a difference, a very great difference. In this case the character of the river at that point is being changed. The ordinary mode of crossing by boat is necessarily being considerably affected, and I felt that the government, having been obliged to spend a considerable amount of money in building a service bridge for the operation of the lock and lifting curtains, it would not he unreasonable to go a little further and, .instead of compelling the 'municipality to build the approaches, do that work ourselves.

I do not wish the minister to think for a moment that I am objecting. I think it is a very good idea to provide this service bridge for the people, because the municipalities contiguous to this portion of the river would certainly he put to a very large expense to erect a bridge. But I am rather amused at the reason the hon. minister has given, that the erection of this dam is going to interfere with the crossing of the river by a ferry. However. I do not wish to make any objection. I think the idea is a very good one.
What will he the increased cost to make the provision for the municipality 1

$63,000 is the estimate.
Mr. ME1GHEN. I understand the minister to say that the present vote of $55,000 will
complete the opening of the river for all the purposes of navigation, but will not complete the bridge?

This will complete the payments under the existing contracts, hut will not complete the approaches to the bridge or the sodding.
So the amount I was then asking the committee for was the amopnt required to complete the payments bn the bridge. I said as plainly as any words could say it that if we were to go on with the approaches and to complete the sodding we would have to get a further vote.
Will the minister read the other portion, which is marked, and say what inference he would draw from it?
I shall read all the passages that are marked:

The government has been engaged for some time in building a lock and dam at St. Andrew's rapids for the purpose of affording navigation from Lake Winnipeg to the city of Winnipeg. The work is now practically completed, and we expect that in a few days it will be open for navigation.

Does the hon. minister purpose completing the roadway across this superstructure, which I understand is intended to be used as a municipal road? Does he propose making connections with the banks on either side?

What my hon. friend, I suppose, means is, shall we build the approaches so as to enable tbe people to avail themselves of the bridge which was built primarily as a service bridge for the lock and dam, as a highway bridge. I may say that we intend to do so.
I was not asking for a vote then for that purpose. I did not say that we were going to do it now. It was intimated as clearly as words could intimate that the vote for which we were then asking would not enable us to do it, and clearly the hon. gentleman who heard me must have understood that we would have to come back again to parliament for a vote which would enable us to build the approaches and to do the sodding if we so decided. Afterwards, if I remember rightly, we did come for authority to do the sodding.

I want to emphasize what I said. The minister read a portion of the ' Hansard,' which I admit I did not notice, but it would not have made any difference in the construction I placed on the portion of his remarks which I read. I was not in the House and my attention was drawn to it, and I submit that no other inference could be drawn by any fair-minded man. than the inference I drew. After the , hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr Meighen) had asked to have the matter stand, the minister said:

I would he very glad to. Both of these hon. gentlemen have already

spoken on the question, and I am sure that they would regret that there should be any delay in the passing of the item. The member for Selkirk a short time ago spoke in very strong terms of the importance of finishing up these approaches and of the very great importance of the work.
I would like to know if it is not fair for me to infer that the minister meant us to understand, and I am sure the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the other members must have felt that the minister was providing some part of the money necessary to complete the approaches to that great work. The Dominion of Canada has expended large amounts there. I understand it has already cost $1,500,000.
That was for purposes *of navigation.

The bridge is there, [DOT]concreted, all ready for use; all it wants is the two approaches, which I understand will cost $60,000 or $70,000. Is it possible that the minister is going to allow that magnificent structure to stand there without those approaches, which will enable this work to be used, and allow it to rust year after year?

Allow me to correct any error into which mv hon. friend has inadvertently fallen. He said the highway bridge cost $200,000 ; but my information from the engineering branch of the department is that such is not the case. We have [DOT]constructed a service bridge for the purpose [DOT]of operating the curtains.and that service bridge cost $200,000, but the extra cost of preparing it as a highway bridge only represents $50,000.

I will not argue that point, but as I have already stated I myself investigated the matter when the work was under construction, and one of the .resident engineers informed me that the providing of the highway bridge involved an extra cost of something like $200,000, and he figured it that while the service bridge was an absolute necessity for raising the *curtains, the steel work in connection with it had to be made so much stronger for a highway bridge that it occasioned the extra cost. However, that is aside from the question ; the bridge is there. Is the minister going to allow it to stand there idle? I appeal to him now to complete that work. It is of absolute necessity to the welfare [DOT]of that district. The country has spent one [DOT]and a half million dollars constructing the work and surely the people should not be -denied the advantages which would accrue by the completion of this bridge at an [DOT]extra expenditure of $50,000 or $60,000. As it stands at present it is a disgrace to this government. Does the minister intend to provide a sum in the estimates to implement the pledge in regard to this matter Mr. PUGSLEY.
which he gave across the floor of the House last year?
The estimates must speak for themselves when they are brought down. I regret I am not able to give the information ; I have no authority to say what council will do.

It seems to me that the term ' service bridge ' is a bit of a joke when applied to a bridge that is of no service to anybody. I notice that in these estimates there is $174,000 all told allocated to poor little Manitoba, and I feel that it is necessary for some one from that province to draw the attention of the government to the fact that Manitoba is not getting its just due in the matter of public expenditure. For instance, in. Nova Scotia these estimates provide for an expenditure of $938,230, and in New Brunswick for an expenditure of $1,323,950, while at. the present moment Manitoba has a greater population than either of the other two. But, New Brunswick represented by the Minister of Public Works gets $1,323,950 expended within its boundaries while poor little Manitoba is only to get $174,000. It is the most scandalous thing which has ever been shown up in this House. -What is the reason of it. Is it bribery, is it corruption, or is it reward? It is a most scandalous piece of what I call parliamentary corruption, and jobbery. I want to know from the Minister of Public Works why Manitoba is treated in that way. Is it because Manitoba sent eight Conservative members here, and only two to support the government? Let me tell the minister if he does'nt know it-and he never knows anything that is pertinent to the question before the House unless it suits him-let me tell him that in 1901 the population of Manitoba was about 500,000, the population of Nova 'Scotia 459,000, and the population of New Brunswick 331,120. I hope it is not my remarks that make the minister yawn. I want some accounting from the minister for this. Is Manitoba being punished, is New Brunswick being rewarded? I want a fair, square answer if it is possible to get it from the Minister of Public Works.
The hon. gentleman is so unconscious of the meaning of some observations that he makes, that I will not take offence.
I do not think you could.
If these remarks were made by some hon. gentlemen I would take offence, but we have to give to the hon. and picturesque member from one of the Manitoba constituencies a good deal of latitude.

I do not want any privilege in this House except the privi-

lege of any honourable, decent member. I have made a proposition to the minister, and I ask him to answer it, as one man to another man on honourable grounds.

The committee tolerates a good deal from the bon. gentleman, and I will not depart from what has been the custom of the committee and this House in regard to him. Therefore, I will endeavour to make a courteous answer. He asks in regard to the expenses in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick compared with those in Manitoba. As far as New Brunswick is concerned, there are no expenses being made which are not in my judgment absolutely necessary in the public interest. We are making provision at the port of St. John for accommodating the national traffic which is coming to that port. The city of St. John began some 14 years ago to make improvements. The people taxed themselves to the extent of a million and -a quarter dollars, to provide terminal facilities. The business has increased enormously, and last year the exports at that port reached $25,000,000. Then, it has been necessary to build wharfs at various places throughout the province for the accommodation of shipping. Public buildings we are only putting up where they are necessary. So far as the province of Manitoba is concerned, while the appropriations for this year are not large, we completed only recently, at a cost of a million and a quarter dollars, a work at St. Andrew's rapids which I believe, is going to be of paramount importance to the city of Winnipeg and to the province of Manitoba generally. We have erected in the city of Winnipeg a magnificent post office building, a magnificent customs warehouse and an immigration building. We have erected a public building at Brandon, and we are proceeding to erect one at Portage la Prairie. We are also putting up public buildings at Souris. We have erected public buildings at Emerson, Dauphin and other places. There are no great harbours to dredge in Manitoba, but we are doing dredging on Lake Winnipeg, on Lake Manitoba and in the Red river. Then we have in prospect the building in the near future of the Hudson Bay railway, which, if the boundaries of the province of Manitoba are extended, as we expect they will be to Hudson Bay, will be built wholly in the province of Manitoba. There will be an expenditure on that railway reaching upwards of $20,000,000, made wholly in the province of Manitoba, and when the railway reaches either Fort Churchill or Fort Nelson, I expect that we shall be called upon to expend, not hundreds of thousands, but probably millions of dollars in the improvement of the harbour, giving facilities for, I hope, an enormous traffic that will flow from Manitoba and
the other western provinces, by way of this short line, to the markets of the old world. We have made surveys of the Saskatchewan river, and if we carry out the works which those surveys seem to warrant, we shall have to build dams at various points along the route in order to bring Winnipeg into water communication with Prince Albert -and Edmonton and right on to the foothfils of the Rocky Mountains. I trust that the hon. gentleman will not be sectional in this matter, for we hope to make improvements in that province even beyond his most sanguine anticipations.

I do not know that I can take much exception to the opening words of the minister, in which he referred to me as a picturesque member. I think I would rather be called a picturesque member than an unctuous member. Beyond those few personal words, I do not see the bearing of what he has said. He refers to what he expects to do on the Saskatchewan river. What has that to do with Manitoba ? He refers to the expenditure he proposes to make in Portage la Prairie that does not help us, because the expenditure has not been made. He refers to the possibilities of Fort Churchill. What has that to do with Manitoba as at present constituted ? Perhaps the minister will tell us that the efforts of the provincial ministers who have come down here have resulted favourably, and that Fort Churchill is going to be in Manitoba. If that is the case, I will welcome any^ expenditures that he makes in that direction. I only opened this subject because as a Manitoban I object to__my province being so neglected by the minister as the blue-books show.
What works does the hon. gentleman ask for ?

I ask for a fair per capita expenditure of public money. We find that the government of Canada is spending 34 cents per head in Manitoba, while it is spending $2 per head in Nova Scotia and $4 per head in the province of the Minister of Public Works. Where is the justice of that ? All I ask is justice and fair play all around.

Before this item passes, and in view of the remarks which the Minister of Public Works dropped a moment ago, I am sure he will pardon me if I say a few words on behalf of the constituency I represent, more particularly as he certainly cannot accuse me of imposing my views on him too frequently or of urging him to undertake unnecessary public expenditure within the borders of my constituency. Since he has seen fit to refer to some works he has had built within the borders of the province of Manitoba, let me refer him to
I think that Manitoba is pretty fairly served in public buildings, judging by the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche).
What does the minister think about Marquette? Has that been fairly served?
That is only one, and, of course, the hon. gentleman's own friends would oppose any expenditure there, because they condemn expenditures in towns of 1,700 of population.
But there are towns under 1,700 to which the hon. minister has given public buildings.	.
But hon. gentlemen opposite have protested most indignantly against this.

Some of the items went through with very little criticism, indeed, and for towns with less population. Therefore, I think that Minnedosa, which is a railway centre, and is developing a large water-power, and which is becoming a summer resort, and is likewise a judicial centre, or shire town, in which the provincial government _ have erected a $40,000 court house and jail, certainly deserves the attention of the minister far more than some of those other insignificant places which he has favoured. I would urge the Minister of Public Works to carefully eon-siaer_ my representations and see that justice is done the town of Minnedosa in the future, and not pass it over in favour of towns much less important, more especially in view of the record his government has had in connection with the constituency of Marquette since I have had the honour of representing it.

I think the request of my hon. friend very reasonable, and if I had the money available it would give me great pleasure to accede to it. more particularly as the hon. gentleman is very reasonable at all times in the representations he makes to the House. I think he has made out a strong case. He has pointed out that Minnedosa is a shire town, that, it is a thriving place, and that there is no public building in the constituency. So that certainly I shall take his remarks carefully into consideration with a view of seeing whether or not it is possible to meet his request.
My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) must feel his hopes raised to the very zenith by these remarks of the Minister of Public Works.
The member for Marquette seems to be quite able to take care of himself.

I am sorry that the minister fails to understand what I am saying. When the hon. minister tells my hon. friend that he will take this into his consideration, it may, in the course of a year, get into his estimates. Then when the hon. member is returned again, if the minister follows his record in other constituencies, in about four years more he may possibly start the building. So it is the duty of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) to communicate the good news to his constituents that within five years there is a possibility of a start being made on a post office at Minnedosa. What I complain of is, not only -what has been pointed out by the hon. member for Dauphin, that there are in the estimates only 34 cents per man in Manitoba, while there are $2 for Nova Scotia, and $4 for New Brunswick ; but also that the items in the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia estimates, so far as they cover constituencies represented by friends of the .government, are live estimates, and are being actually spent; while the Manitoba estimates are dead estimates, waiting for the elections. For every dollar that is spent per man in the province of Manitoba there are $6 spent in Nova Scotia and $12 spent in New Brunswick.- If we leave out the class of expenditures the minister refers to, namely, those that in some sense serve the whole of Canada and are chargeable to capital, the fact still remains that for $1 spent in Manitoba there are $8 spent in Nova Scotia and $8 in New Brunswick. Leaving out that class, it would not be unfair for us to ask the minister to observe some due proportion between these three provinces. The minister knows enough about the duty of a member to his constituency to know that he cannot expect members on this side of the House to sit quietly in their seats while he performs a gross injustice to the nrovince he represents. In the constituency of Portage la Prairie the hon. gentleman did, during the time it was represented by a friend of me government, build a post office at Neepawa. The post office was erected in a location to suit the party rather than to suit the town. Now the other estimate that was put in for Portage la Prairie was also a pre-election estimate. The minister placed the item in the estimates in 1907-8, he dropped it immediately the elections were over. Subsequently he was prevailed upon to reinstate it, on the general principle which he then laid down that all the estimates of 1907-8 had a prior claim on the attention of his department. The site was purchased, and it still stands I believe in the name of the government; but there the whole matter rests. I have communicated with the minister, petitions have been urging the matter, but somehow they land in the vermiform appendix of the government and never seem

to get through. I do not need to call the attention of the minister to the necessities there. The minister has acknowledged them years ago, they have grown in importance since the number of regiments has been increased by one, making two now. The building that they are trying to use at present would be discreditable to a Chinaman. One is in grave danger of breaking his leg if he tries to enter it. It is an eyesore on the street, it would not be looked upon with credit in the most dilapidated and forsaken spot in the universe. Now there is a considerable interest being taken in military matters in that city, it has grown by leaps and bounds. Indeed, one of the chief promoters, and one of those most thoroughly imbued with the military spirit, is the representative in the local House on the opposition side for that constituency. I am sure that gentleman will use his influence with the minister, and I will assist him all I cantourgetheminister to forward that work. I have brought to bear upon the minister every influence of a legitimate character that I could think of to urge forward this building. It is at present in an embryo state, the working plans I believe are under way. But I want to ask the minister if he can suggest anything further I can do as a representative of that constituency to hurry on the completion. of this work.
Is the hon. gentleman a typesetter?
No, I am not.

Then the hon. gentleman cannot help the matter at all, because the specifications are now being printed. They will be ready in about a fortnight, when tenders will be called for by public advertisement.

I want to put in another word for Manitoba. Manitoba wants a great deal. Now, when so much money is being voted, only $170,000 for Manitoba and over $1,300,000 for the province the Minister of Public Works comes from, with onlv two-thirds of the population of Manitoba, surely Manitoba is not being treated justly. We are asking for all kinds of things of Manitoba not in a partisan way, but for the benefit of the province; we are asking for $2,500,000 for an exposition in Winnipeg. This is not a political matter, it is a nlan for the benefit of the province, for the benefit of all Canada, as we believe. Can we not get some assurance from the minister that he will further our desires in that regard?

The matter of aid to the exhibition is under consideration. My hon. friend would not expect me to inform him in advance as to whether the decision of the government will be favourable or other-Mr. MEIGHEN.
wise. I regret I am. not able to give him any information on the subject.
Winnipeg 'military buildings, hospital,. $13,000.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) want that to stand?

No. I think this would be a proper time to bring up the question as to the Winnipeg armoury. No doubt it has been brought to Hie attention of the minister many times and strongly urged upon him. We have, I think, during the past year, two new regiments, and they have not facilities for even storing their regimental equipment. I had fully expected tc see an item in the estimates in connection "with this. While answering that Question, the minister might also make a statement that, I Jim sure, will be received with interest by the people of Winnipeg. He is aware of the situation of the parliament buildings there. They are old, out-of-date, unsanitary. They occupy a part of one block, the other part of which is occupied by the barracks and drill shed. I believe it has been the desire of the local government to -acquire the portion occupied by the Dominion government with the barracks and drill shed m order to have an area upon which to put up proper parliamentary buildings for the province. We would then have what could be made a modest but very nice little park, bounded by Broad-way, Osborne and Kennedy streets, and, upon the south, by the Assinboine river. I would like to know from the minister if there is an intention on the part of the government to act in that way?

With regard to the drill-shed, I think I am right in saying that the proposed exchange of properties would not-affect the site of the drill shed-I take it that it could be built on the same property. The question of building a new drill shed has not been recently brought to my attention. I am not aware whether complaints have been made as to the accommodation afforded by the drill shed. I will have it. looked into, and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) will mention it when the Minister of Militia is here-for there-are items for military buildings that have been left over-I can assure my hon. friend that he will not be held down to technical rules, but, if Mr. Chairman and the members of the committee are willing, he will be. afforded facilities for getting the information he desires. As to the proposed exchange, I understood that the communications between the provincial government and this government took place, so far as our side is concerned, with the Militia Department. They have not been brought to-

my notice, and I have no further information than what I have seen in the newspapers. It is not unlikely that the Minister of Militia will bring this matter to 'my attention shortly. I will ask my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart, Winnipeg) to be good enough, when some of these buildings are under consideration, to mention this matter as well. I have no doubt the Minister of Militia will give as full information as he is able to do with regard to the negotiations.	'
With regard to the item under discussion, I suppose we are to understand that this hospital, wherever it is to be built, will not be built on the present military property in the city of Winnipeg?
It will not be built in such a way as to interfere at all with the negotiations. That will be very important, of course.

A very important matter has been brought to the attention of the minister with regard to the way Manitoba is treated by this government. Looking through the estimates, we find item 141, which shows that Manitoba is getting the paltry sum of $73,000 for public buildings for the whole province. A few years ago, when we had quite a number of gentlemen from that province occupying seats on the other side of the House, we saw that Manitoba was a good deal better treated than it is to-day. If we look at the next item, No. 142, we find that Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories receive $584,000. These items should, to a certain extent, take into consideration the amount of revenue collected in the several provinces. If you look at the figures you find that Manitoba pays into the Dominion treasury between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000 a year, which is a good deal more than double what is paid in by both these provinces put together. And when you analyse the amount that is being spent in these two provinces you see that almost every man occupying a seat on the other side of the House is being taken care of in splendid shape. I do not think it is right that we should be treated in that way. In my own constituency we have several towns a good deal better than the town of Humboldt, for instance, yet we see that Humboldt gets a new building worth about $25,000 or $30,000. They are renting a building there at the present time for $280 a year that fulfils the conditions necessary for that town, or, at least, has fulfilled them in the past. Under this expenditure in Humboldt we shall be paying-taking the money at six per cent-instead of $280 a year, about $1,500 a year. We have not a single public building in my whole constituency, and we have several towns there a good deal more entitled to it, I think- and I believe the minister would acknowledge that if he would look into the case- than even this town of Humboldt. I think these Dublic buildings should be more fairly distributed among the different provinces and among the various constituencies.

I think we have made exceedingly good progress to-day. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
